## Summary

Eisman explains the crisis through leverage, deteriorating mortgage quality, concentration of exposures and derivative connections. His strongest analytical lessons are that leverage can masquerade as operating skill, historical loss models can fail when underwriting changes, and like-aged loan vintages reveal deterioration hidden by aggregates. Primary research supports these mechanisms. His account overstates a universal risk-weighting explanation and misdescribes typical subprime introductory rates. Loan-level evidence also complicates his reset-centered causal chain. The blanket claim that real household incomes stopped growing in the early 1990s is contradicted by Census data.

Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.

## Material claims

<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c001"></a>
### 001. The crisis combined excessive leverage, a collapsing mortgage asset class, concentrated exposure at systemic institutions and opaque derivative links.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 2:09-3:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=129s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Primary research and the commission investigation support the interacting leverage, common-exposure and funding mechanisms. This is a useful broad diagnosis, not proof that these exhaust every cause.

Assessment test: Trace losses, funding and counterparty exposures across major institutions.

- [Financial Statistics for the United States and the Crisis](https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2010/201020/index.html) (2010-04-15): Research identifies leverage, short-term funding and shared exposures as core vulnerabilities. Loan-vintage data show worsening early-payment defaults, reaching about 8% for 2007 loans within one year, and explain why aggregate data can conceal risk.
- [Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13](https://fcic-static.law.stanford.edu/cdn_media/fcic-reports/fcic_final_report_full.pdf) (2011-01-27): Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c002"></a>
### 002. Lenders do not know eventual loan losses when they originate credit, so apparent profitability depends on uncertain loss estimates.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | analytical principle | major

[Source at 3:05-4:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=185s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Future defaults and recoveries are unknown at origination. Replacing an expected loss with the realized loss can change reported lifetime profitability, even with unchanged contractual interest.

Conditional reasoning: Future defaults and recoveries are unknown at origination. Replacing an expected loss with the realized loss can change reported lifetime profitability, even with unchanged contractual interest.

Assessment test: Compare origination loss estimates with vintage lifetime defaults and recoveries.


<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c003"></a>
### 003. For consistent income, asset and equity definitions, return on equity equals return on assets multiplied by assets-to-equity leverage.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 4:59-7:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=299s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

(Net income/assets)*(assets/equity)=net income/equity, for nonzero assets and equity with matching measurement periods. This is an identity, not an assurance that ROA remains constant when leverage changes.

Conditional reasoning: (Net income/assets)*(assets/equity)=net income/equity, for nonzero assets and equity with matching measurement periods. This is an identity, not an assurance that ROA remains constant when leverage changes.

Assessment test: Reconcile average balances and capital definitions before applying the identity.


<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c004"></a>
### 004. Deposits are bank liabilities, and adding deposit-funded assets can raise equity returns even without improving return on assets.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 7:18-10:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=438s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

In the stated examples ROA is fixed after deposit interest expense. Increasing assets relative to unchanged equity therefore increases ROE. Real funding costs and risk can alter ROA.

Conditional reasoning: In the stated examples ROA is fixed after deposit interest expense. Increasing assets relative to unchanged equity therefore increases ROE. Real funding costs and risk can alter ROA.

Assessment test: Hold the stated net ROA assumption fixed for the illustration; assess funding costs separately in actual banks.


<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c005"></a>
### 005. Compensation tied to earnings and ROE creates incentives to increase leverage, requiring restraint rather than assuming managers will self-limit.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 10:00-10:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=600s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The investigation documents asymmetric pay and ROE-based rewards that encouraged leverage and short-term risk. It does not establish that regulators are the only possible restraint.

Assessment test: Inspect incentive contracts, deferred compensation, clawbacks and actual leverage decisions.

- [Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13](https://fcic-static.law.stanford.edu/cdn_media/fcic-reports/fcic_final_report_full.pdf) (2011-01-27): Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.

<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c006"></a>
### 006. At one hundred times assets to equity, a loss of one percent of assets wipes out the original equity buffer.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 10:44-11:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=644s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

With assets 100 and equity 1, a loss of 1 reduces equity to zero, assuming no offsetting income or capital issuance and no change in liabilities.

Conditional reasoning: With assets 100 and equity 1, a loss of 1 reduces equity to zero, assuming no offsetting income or capital issuance and no change in liabilities.

Assessment test: Calculate losses relative to the actual common-equity loss-absorbing buffer.

### 007. Some bank leverage is economically useful because deposit intermediation supports lending at affordable rates; the policy problem is the appropriate amount.

<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c010"></a>
### 010. Risk weighting is intended to distinguish the capital needs of portfolios with different credit risk rather than treating equal asset amounts as equally risky.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 13:54-15:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=834s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The Federal Reserve paper describes risk-sensitive capital rules and contrasts them with simple leverage limits. Actual regulatory capital definitions are more complex than the lecture’s common-equity shorthand.

Assessment test: Map asset risk weights and qualifying capital definitions under each applicable regime.

- [Competitive Effects of Risk-Based Bank Capital Regulation](https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2006/200646/index.html) (2006-08): Describes Basel I mortgage capital rules, proposed Basel II internal default/loss estimates, and separate non-risk-weighted leverage limits. Regulatory capital is not simply common equity and risk weights were not all delegated to external rating agencies.

<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c011"></a>
### 011. Rating agencies largely determine risk weights, and regulatory capital and leverage ratios are all calculated on a risk-weighted basis.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 18:04-21:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=1084s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

External ratings matter for some securities, but the primary regulatory description includes prescribed weights, bank internal estimates and separate non-risk-based leverage limits. The universal description is inaccurate.

Assessment test: Identify the jurisdiction, bank type, date and applicable standardized or internal-model capital approach.

- [Competitive Effects of Risk-Based Bank Capital Regulation](https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2006/200646/index.html) (2006-08): Describes Basel I mortgage capital rules, proposed Basel II internal default/loss estimates, and separate non-risk-weighted leverage limits. Regulatory capital is not simply common equity and risk weights were not all delegated to external rating agencies.

<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c012"></a>
### 012. Adding low-risk-weight assets can increase simple balance-sheet leverage without materially weakening the reported risk-weighted capital ratio.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 18:40-19:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=1120s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

For fixed capital, adding assets with zero weight increases gross assets without increasing RWA; adding low-weight assets can likewise increase gross leverage disproportionately. This demonstrates the mechanism, not its prevalence.

Conditional reasoning: For fixed capital, adding assets with zero weight increases gross assets without increasing RWA; adding low-weight assets can likewise increase gross leverage disproportionately. This demonstrates the mechanism, not its prevalence.

Assessment test: Compare changes in total assets, RWA, risk weights and loss-absorbing capital.


<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c013"></a>
### 013. Historical loss patterns can become misleading when lending standards loosen, because deteriorating loans take time to season into losses.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 19:25-20:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=1165s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Loan-vintage research documents deterioration concealed by favorable aggregate conditions and emphasizes granular credit analysis. The timing and magnitude cannot be inferred from past averages alone.

Assessment test: Track like-aged vintages and underwriting variables rather than relying on aggregate trailing losses.

- [Financial Statistics for the United States and the Crisis](https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2010/201020/index.html) (2010-04-15): Research identifies leverage, short-term funding and shared exposures as core vulnerabilities. Loan-vintage data show worsening early-payment defaults, reaching about 8% for 2007 loans within one year, and explain why aggregate data can conceal risk.
- [Ten Myths about Subprime Mortgages](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2009/ec-20090509-ten-myths-about-subprime-mortgages) (2009-05-09): Author summarizes her loan-level research: initial subprime hybrid rates averaged 7.3-9.7% in 2001-2007; fixed and adjustable loans both deteriorated by vintage. Rising prices masked worsening quality. Subprime classification was not determined solely by FICO.

<a id="4bSCdJTbR8I-c017"></a>
### 017. Real incomes for most Americans stopped increasing in the early 1990s and remain stagnant in that sense today.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | material factual premise | supporting

[Source at 24:40-25:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=1480s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Census real median household income rose from $64,240 in 1993 to $73,760 in 1999, $74,810 in 2007 and $85,210 in 2024 in the inspected consistent-dollar series. Long plateaus do not justify the blanket no-growth claim. The series is not individual longitudinal income.

Assessment test: Specify household versus individual income and measure the relevant distribution over the claimed period.

- [Real Median Household Income in the United States](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/MEHOINUSA672N) (2026-09-16): Inflation-adjusted median household income in 2025 dollars: 1993 $64,240; 1999 $73,760; 2007 $74,810; 2019 $85,320; 2024 $85,210; 2025 $87,460. Not a longitudinal measure of each household.

### 030. Rolling refinancing fees into principal can prevent a borrower from paying down the mortgage despite making payments.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 35:19-36:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=2119s) | Stance: conditional | Horizon: not stated

If capitalized refinancing costs equal or exceed principal repaid since the previous refinancing, the new balance is at least the prior balance. This requires the stated fee and amortization relationship and is not universal.

Conditional reasoning: If capitalized refinancing costs equal or exceed principal repaid since the previous refinancing, the new balance is at least the prior balance. This requires the stated fee and amortization relationship and is not universal.

Assessment test: Compare amortization actually paid with fees and cash-out added to each replacement loan.

- [Ten Myths about Subprime Mortgages](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2009/ec-20090509-ten-myths-about-subprime-mortgages) (2009-05-09): Author summarizes her loan-level research: initial subprime hybrid rates averaged 7.3-9.7% in 2001-2007; fixed and adjustable loans both deteriorated by vintage. Rising prices masked worsening quality. Subprime classification was not determined solely by FICO.
- [Financial Statistics for the United States and the Crisis](https://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2010/201020/index.html) (2010-04-15): Research identifies leverage, short-term funding and shared exposures as core vulnerabilities. Loan-vintage data show worsening early-payment defaults, reaching about 8% for 2007 loans within one year, and explain why aggregate data can conceal risk.

### 036. The 2007 investor strike shut the securitization channel, reduced new lending and refinancing, and worsened mortgage distress.

**Mixed** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 40:58-41:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4bSCdJTbR8I&t=2458s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Funding interruption and refinancing feedback are supported by the investigation. The reset-centered chain is incomplete: loan-level research finds pre-reset distress and similarly worsening fixed-rate vintages. It cannot explain the crisis solely as borrowers moving from 3% to 9%.

Assessment test: Decompose defaults by vintage, product, reset timing, income shocks and refinancing availability.

- [Financial Crisis Inquiry Report, findings and chapters 4, 6, 7, 13](https://fcic-static.law.stanford.edu/cdn_media/fcic-reports/fcic_final_report_full.pdf) (2011-01-27): Investigative evidence documents fragile leverage/funding, fee and ROE incentives, deteriorating underwriting, and securitization dependence. Pages 61-64 describe pay incentives; pages 89 and 125 describe the origination chain; page 281 reports Bear near 38:1 and balance-sheet window dressing. Findings are not proof of a single exclusive cause.
- [Ten Myths about Subprime Mortgages](https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/economic-commentary/2009/ec-20090509-ten-myths-about-subprime-mortgages) (2009-05-09): Author summarizes her loan-level research: initial subprime hybrid rates averaged 7.3-9.7% in 2001-2007; fixed and adjustable loans both deteriorated by vintage. Rising prices masked worsening quality. Subprime classification was not determined solely by FICO.

## Framework and tools

- Decompose ROE into asset profitability and leverage.
- Treat estimated loan losses as uncertain costs rather than immediately known margins.
- Question historical risk weights when underwriting changes.
- Compare loan vintages at equal seasoning and account for tax-refund seasonality.
- Choose a short instrument with manageable liquidity, borrow costs and capacity.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Illustrative banks with $1 billion equity and 1x, 10x and 100x assets/equity
- ROA, ROE and risk-weighted capital ratios
- Historical bank leverage and subprime origination volumes
- Low/no-documentation share and hybrid mortgage refinancing
- Monthly securitization delinquency, repossession and loss reports by vintage

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
- The opening montage repeats later material.
- Illustrative bank balance sheets expressly omit liquidity and hold ROA constant.
- He calls 2000 a recession year and gives simplified industry chronology; incidental chronology is not used to judge the investment thesis.
- The repeated 3% initial subprime rate is load-bearing in the refinancing explanation and is preserved rather than silently corrected.
